means: Traffic arriving faster than you can process it, and the system deliberately pushing back instead of silently piling up.
example: Flash sale: 500,000 checkout hits in 10 seconds, capacity is 10,000/sec. The system queues, sheds, or slows accepts. Without backpressure the queue grows until memory dies.
diagram:
Arrival: ████████████████████
Capacity: ████████
              ↓
    Queue → Delay → Shed load
    (signal the producer to slow down)

means: Writing up an incident to fix the system, not to identify who to punish. Blame makes people hide information, which makes the next outage worse.
example: 'Engineer ran the wrong migration' becomes 'Migrations run against prod with no confirmation prompt and no dry-run.' The second version generates fixes.
diagram:
Blame:     who did it → hiding → repeat
Blameless: what allowed it → guardrail

Output = action items with owners,
not a name

means: How much of the system (or how many users) a single failure can take down. Every architecture decision either grows or shrinks it.
example: One shared DB for all tenants: blast radius = everyone. Sharded per region: blast radius = one region. Canary at 5%: blast radius = 5%.
diagram:
Shared everything → 100% of users
Per-region shard   → 1 region
Cell architecture  → 1 cell
Canary 5%          → 5%

means: Two identical production environments. Deploy to the idle one, verify, then flip all traffic at the load balancer. Rollback is another flip.
example: Blue serves live traffic. v2 goes to green, smoke tests pass, the LB switches. A bad release is undone in seconds instead of a redeploy.
diagram:
LB
       │ (flip)
  ┌────┴────┐
BLUE v1   GREEN v2
 live      idle → tested → live

Rollback = flip back

means: Isolate resources per dependency so one slow thing can't drink the whole pool. Named after ship compartments.
example: One shared 50-connection pool. The reporting DB hangs, 50 threads block on it, and login breaks too. With bulkheads: reporting gets 10 connections, auth gets 20 — reporting dies alone.
diagram:
Shared pool:    [50] → reporting hangs → all dead
Bulkheaded:
  auth      [20]  ✓ still serving
  reporting [10]  ✗ contained
  search    [20]  ✓ still serving

means: How fast you are consuming the error budget relative to normal. The alert that actually pages people.
example: Burn rate 1x means you'd exactly use the budget by month end. Burn rate 14.4x means the whole monthly budget is gone in two hours — page immediately.
diagram:
1x    → on track, no alert
6x     → budget gone in 5 days → ticket
14.4x  → budget gone in 2 hrs  → page now

Alert on burn rate, not raw error count

means: The thundering herd applied to caches, plus the fix: only one caller recomputes while everyone else waits or serves stale.
example: Instead of 8,000 recomputes, the first miss takes a lock and refreshes; the other 7,999 get the slightly stale value. One DB query instead of 8,000.
diagram:
Miss → acquire lock?
  YES → recompute → store → serve
  NO  → serve stale / wait for holder

1 recompute, not 8000

means: Release new code to a small slice of traffic first, watch the metrics, then expand.
example: New recommendation model goes to 5% of users. Error rate and latency hold for 20 minutes, so it rolls to 100%. If it had spiked, only 5% were affected.
diagram:
v2 → 5% traffic → observe 20 min
       ↓ healthy        ↓ regression
    25% → 100%        rollback
                     (5% blast radius)

means: Deliberately injecting failure in production-like conditions to verify your resilience actually works before reality tests it.
example: You kill a random pod during business hours to confirm the failover you designed a year ago still fires. Half the time, it doesn't.
diagram:
Hypothesis: killing 1 replica = no user impact
   ↓ inject failure
   ↓ measure SLI
Matched?  → confidence earned
Diverged? → you just found a bug for free

means: Stops your system from repeatedly calling a service that is already failing. Like a fuse — it trips before everything burns.
example: Payment API starts failing. Without a breaker the app retries endlessly and takes the whole process down. With one, failures are counted, the breaker opens, and a fallback is served.
diagram:
CLOSED  → calls pass, failures counted
   ↓ threshold hit
OPEN    → fail fast, no calls made
   ↓ cool-down elapsed
HALF-OPEN → let 1 probe through
   ↓ success        ↓ failure
 CLOSED           OPEN

means: Extra delay when a server, container or function starts from scratch after being idle.
example: A Lambda sits idle 30 minutes. Next request loads the runtime, imports dependencies, loads the model. User waits 6s instead of 0.3s.
diagram:
Request arrives
  ↓ load runtime
  ↓ load dependencies
  ↓ load model
  ↓ init connections
Response (finally) — 6s

means: How much failure you're allowed before breaching the SLO. It converts reliability into a currency the team can spend on shipping speed.
example: 99.9% monthly SLO = 43 minutes of downtime allowed. A week-1 incident burns 20. With 23 left, the team freezes risky deploys until the window resets.
diagram:
Budget: 43 min/month
  incident −20 min
  remaining 23 min
     ↓
healthy budget → ship fast
burnt budget   → freeze, fix reliability

means: The thing message brokers cannot actually give you over a network. What you get is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which behaves like exactly-once.
example: RabbitMQ redelivers a message after a consumer crashes post-work, pre-ack. The work runs twice. Only your dedupe table makes the outcome once.
diagram:
At-most-once  → may lose
At-least-once → may duplicate  ← reality
Exactly-once  → at-least-once
                + idempotent consumer

means: Wait longer after each failed retry, with randomness added so clients don't all retry on the same tick.
example: 1000 clients fail at the same instant. Fixed backoff means 1000 retries hit at exactly t+1s — a synchronized wave. Jitter spreads them randomly across the window.
diagram:
No jitter:  ▮        ▮        ▮   (thundering)
Jitter:     ▪ ▪  ▪ ▪▪   ▪  ▪ ▪   (spread)

sleep = random(0, base * 2^attempt)

means: Turn behaviour on or off without redeploying. Separates deploy (shipping code) from release (exposing it).
example: New summarisation feature ships behind a flag that is off. On for internal team, bugs fixed, on for 10%, then 100%. No deployment at any step.
diagram:
Deploy code (flag OFF) — nobody sees it
  ↓ internal ON  → dogfood
  ↓ 10% ON       → watch metrics
  ↓ 100% ON      → released
Kill switch = flip OFF, zero deploys

means: The reality that database changes usually can't be rolled back with the code. Schema changes must be backward compatible so old and new code can both run.
example: Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it breaks rollback instantly. Instead: stop writing it (release 1), drop it (release 2, a week later).
diagram:
✗ one release: stop using + DROP COLUMN
✓ release 1: stop writing, keep column
✓ release 2: verify unused
✓ release 3: DROP COLUMN

Expand → migrate → contract

means: Losing a feature instead of losing the product when a dependency fails.
example: The recommendation service dies. Instead of a 500 on the homepage, the page renders with a static bestsellers list. Users notice worse suggestions, not an outage.
diagram:
Recommender ✗
   ↓
Homepage still renders
Personalised rail → static bestsellers
   ↓
Feature lost, product alive

means: One slow item at the front of a queue stalls everything behind it, even work that would have been instant.
example: A single 400-page PDF sits at the head of the OCR queue for 9 minutes. Two thousand one-page invoices behind it wait, though each takes 200ms.
diagram:
[400-page PDF ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ 9 min][1pg][1pg][1pg]
  ↑ everything behind waits

Fix: separate queues by size class

means: Send a duplicate request to a second replica once the first is slower than P95, then take whichever answers first.
example: Read P99 drops from 1.8s to 240ms by sending a second copy after 100ms. Costs ~5% extra traffic because you only hedge the slow tail.
diagram:
t=0    → replica A
t=95ms → still waiting
t=95ms → also ask replica B
t=140  → B answers → use it, cancel A

+5% load, -85% tail

means: Doing the same operation N times leaves the system in the same state as doing it once. The single most important property for anything involving money or messages.
example: User clicks "Pay ₹500", network hiccups, client retries. Without idempotency: ₹1000 charged. With an idempotency key: the server recognises the key, returns the original result, charges ₹500 once.
diagram:
POST /pay  Idempotency-Key: abc123
   ↓
Key seen before?
  NO  → charge ₹500 → store result
  YES → return stored result (no charge)

means: A client-generated unique ID attached to a mutating request so the server can dedupe retries. Stored with the result, usually for 24h.
example: Stripe requires one on every charge. Your mobile app generates a UUID per checkout attempt and reuses it across all retries of that same attempt — new attempt, new key.
diagram:
Client generates UUID per intent
   ↓
Server: INSERT key ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
   ↓
Inserted? → do the work, save response
Conflict? → replay saved response

means: Rate limiting that smooths instead of bursting. Requests drain at a fixed rate no matter how they arrive.
example: 200 requests arrive in one second against a 10/sec leak. They queue and drain evenly over 20 seconds. Downstream sees a perfectly flat line.
diagram:
in (bursty)  ▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮▮
                  │
               ┌──▼──┐
               │     │ ← queue absorbs the burst
               │     │   full? → drop
               └──┬──┘
                  ▼ fixed 10/s
out               ▪  ▪  ▪  ▪  ▪  ▪

means: Deliberately dropping low-value requests to keep high-value ones alive under overload.
example: During a spike, the API rejects analytics writes and prefetch calls with 503, but keeps checkout and login at full speed. Revenue traffic survives.
diagram:
Overload detected
   ↓
Drop: prefetch, analytics, recommendations
Keep: login, checkout, payments
   ↓
Degraded, but alive

sub: Mean time to recovery / between failures
means: MTTR is how fast you recover; MTBF is how rarely you break. Mature teams optimise MTTR harder, because you cannot prevent all failure.
example: Team A: fails once a quarter, takes 6 hours to fix. Team B: fails weekly, recovers in 4 minutes. Team B has far better availability.
diagram:
A: MTBF 90d, MTTR 6h  → 99.72%
B: MTBF  7d, MTTR 4m  → 99.96%

Fast recovery beats rare failure

means: Different percentiles answer different questions. P50 is the typical user, P95 is your unhappy tail, P99.9 is the one whale customer whose CEO emails yours.
example: A dashboard alerting on P50 stayed green for six weeks while P99 tripled. The retry storm was only visible above P95.
diagram:
P50   → typical user      → product feel
P95   → unhappy tail      → SLO target
P99   → worst 1%          → churn signal
P99.9 → your biggest acct → escalation

means: Capping how many requests a caller can make in a time window, so one client can't starve everyone else.
example: API allows 100 req/min per key. Request 101 gets 429 with a Retry-After header. Your DB never sees the flood.
diagram:
Limit 100/min
Req 1–100 → 200 OK
Req 101+  → 429 + Retry-After: 23
Window rolls → counter resets

means: Retries meant to help end up destroying the system. Every layer multiplies the load on a service that was only slightly sick.
example: DB slows down 20%. Service A retries 5x, B retries 5x, C retries 5x. Traffic multiplies 15x. The DB, which would have recovered on its own, collapses.
diagram:
DB: slightly slow
  A → ×5   B → ×5   C → ×5
             ↓
       traffic × 15
             ↓
        DB dies

means: Replace instances a few at a time so capacity never drops to zero. The default in Kubernetes.
example: 12 pods, maxSurge 2, maxUnavailable 1. New pods come up and pass readiness before old ones are killed. During the roll, both versions serve traffic — your API must tolerate that.
diagram:
[v1][v1][v1][v1]
[v2][v1][v1][v1]
[v2][v2][v1][v1]
[v2][v2][v2][v2]

Both versions live mid-roll

means: The actual measurement your SLO is defined on. Vague SLOs fail because nobody agreed on the SLI.
example: 'The API is fast' is not an SLI. 'Proportion of GET /search requests returning 200 in under 400ms, measured at the load balancer' is.
diagram:
SLI = good events / valid events

good  = status 2xx AND latency < 400ms
valid = all GET /search (excl. health checks)
measured at = load balancer, 1-min buckets

means: Rate limiting that avoids the boundary bug in fixed windows, where a client sneaks 2x the limit across the reset line.
example: Fixed window of 100/min: 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 at 12:00:01 = 200 in two seconds, both 'legal'. A sliding window weights the previous window and blocks it.
diagram:
Fixed:   [100]|[100]  → 200 in 2s ✗
Sliding: weighted overlap
         count = prev*0.9 + curr
         → correctly rejects

means: Your internal target, always stricter than the SLA. The SLA is the floor; the SLO is where you aim so you never touch the floor.
example: SLA to customers is 99.9%. Team SLO is 99.95%. The gap is your safety buffer. Aim exactly at the SLA and you will breach it regularly.
diagram:
SLO 99.95%  ← team targets here
SLA 99.90%  ← customers hold you here
       ↑
   safety buffer

means: Fanning out to many services makes slow responses near-certain. If each call has a 1% chance of being slow, 100 parallel calls are almost guaranteed to contain one.
example: A page fans out to 100 microservices, each with P99 = 1s. The chance all 100 are fast is 0.99^100 ≈ 37%. So 63% of page loads hit at least one 1s call.
diagram:
1 call:   99% fast
100 calls: 0.99^100 = 37% all fast
   ↓
63% of pages hit the tail
Fix: hedged requests, fewer fan-outs

means: Many clients wake up and hit the same resource at exactly the same moment.
example: A popular cache key expires at 12:00:00. In that instant 8,000 in-flight requests all miss and all query the database for the identical row.
diagram:
Key expires at 12:00:00
   ↓
8000 concurrent misses
   ↓
8000 identical DB queries
   ↓
DB CPU 100%

means: Each layer in a call chain gets a slice of the caller's remaining time, so nothing waits longer than the user already has.
example: Gateway timeout is 3s. It passes 2.8s to the service, which passes 2.5s to the DB. Without budgets, a 30s DB timeout keeps working on a request the user abandoned 27 seconds ago.
diagram:
User 3.0s
 └ Gateway  2.8s
    └ Service 2.5s
       └ DB    2.0s

Deadline propagates down the chain

means: The rate-limit algorithm that allows bursts. Tokens refill at a steady rate; each request spends one; an empty bucket means rejection.
example: Bucket holds 100 tokens, refills 10/sec. An idle client can burst 100 requests instantly, then is throttled to 10/sec. Feels generous and still protects you.
diagram:
Bucket [██████████] cap 100
refill +10/sec
request → take 1 token
empty?  → 429

Allows burst, enforces average

means: Too many non-actionable alerts train people to ignore them, including the real one. Every alert should be actionable, urgent and linked to a runbook.
example: A team gets 60 pages a week, 58 self-resolve. When the real outage pages at 3am, on-call silences it out of habit.
diagram:
Every page must be:
  actionable (a human can do something)
  urgent (can't wait for morning)
  documented (runbook linked)

Otherwise → ticket or dashboard, not a page

means: The number of unique label combinations on a metric. High cardinality is what makes a Prometheus instance fall over.
example: Adding `user_id` as a label to a request counter with 2M users creates 2M time series. Prometheus OOMs; the label belongs in a trace or log, not a metric.
diagram:
http_requests{route, method, status}
  20 × 4 × 6 = 480 series ✓

+ user_id (2M users) = 960,000,000 series ✗

High-cardinality identifiers → logs/traces

means: A single ID threaded through every log line, span and message for one user action, so you can reconstruct it end to end.
example: A support ticket includes the request ID from the error page. One query returns every log line across seven services for that exact request.
diagram:
user action → generate/accept request_id
  ↓ every log line includes it
  ↓ propagated to queues, downstream calls
  ↓ shown to the user on error pages

means: A counter only goes up (use rate()). A gauge goes up and down. A histogram buckets observations so you can compute percentiles.
example: Using a gauge for request latency gives you the last value, which is meaningless. A histogram gives you P50/P95/P99 across the whole window.
diagram:
Counter   requests_total     → rate(...[5m])
Gauge     queue_depth        → current value
Histogram request_duration   → quantiles
Summary   client-side quantiles, can't aggregate

means: Following one request across every service it touches, so you can see exactly where the time went.
example: A 9-second search: auth 0.2s, retrieval 1s, reranking 6s, model 1.5s. Logs said 'slow'. The trace named the culprit in one screen.
diagram:
trace abc123 ───────────────────────── 9.0s
├ auth            ▌                     0.2s
├ retrieval       ███                   1.0s
│ └ vector search ██                    0.8s
├ rerank          ████████████████████  6.0s ←
└ model           ████                  1.5s

A tree of parent/child spans, not a flat list.
The indentation is where the time actually went.

means: Google's four: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. If you only get four graphs per service, these are the four.
example: Saturation is the one teams skip and the one that predicts the next outage — a queue growing steadily is a failure that hasn't happened yet.
diagram:
Latency     how slow
Traffic     how much
Errors      how broken
Saturation  how close to the limit ← leading indicator

means: A dashboard should answer a question, not display everything available. Forty panels means nobody reads any of them during an incident.
example: One overview per service with the four golden signals, and drill-downs behind links. Panels ordered so the top row answers 'is it broken?'.
diagram:
Row 1: is it broken? (SLI, error rate)
Row 2: where? (per-endpoint, per-dependency)
Row 3: why? (resources, saturation)

40 panels of everything = read by no one

means: You cannot average P99s across instances. Averaging percentiles is mathematically wrong and hides the worst instance.
example: Three pods report P99 of 100ms, 100ms and 3s. The average says 1.07s; the real fleet-wide P99 must be computed from the raw buckets.
diagram:
avg(P99 per pod)  ✗ meaningless
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum(rate(bucket[5m])) by (le))  ✓

Aggregate the buckets, then compute the quantile

means: `rate()` is per-second average over a window; `increase()` is the total over it. Applying either to a gauge produces nonsense.
example: `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` gives requests per second and handles counter resets on pod restart. Raw `http_requests_total` just climbs forever.
diagram:
counter: ▁▂▃▄▅ (monotonic, resets on restart)
rate(c[5m])     → per-second average ✓
increase(c[1h]) → total in that hour ✓

Never rate() a gauge

means: For every request-driven service, track Rate, Errors and Duration. Three metrics that cover most of what you need.
example: A new service ships with request rate, error rate and latency histogram on day one. That's enough to detect and triage nearly every incident.
diagram:
R  Rate      requests/sec
E  Errors    failed requests/sec
D  Duration  latency distribution

Same three for every service = comparable dashboards

means: Head sampling decides at the start (cheap, may miss the interesting request). Tail sampling decides after seeing the whole trace, so you can always keep errors and slow requests.
example: 1% head sampling misses 99% of the rare 8-second requests you actually want. Tail sampling keeps 100% of errors and slow traces plus 1% of normal ones.
diagram:
Head: decide at request start
  1% kept → rare failures usually missed ✗
Tail: buffer, decide at the end
  keep all errors + all slow + 1% normal ✓
  cost: buffering infrastructure

means: A trace is a tree of spans, each with an ID and a parent. Context must propagate through HTTP headers and message metadata or the trace breaks in half.
example: The trace stops at the queue boundary because traceparent wasn't copied into the message headers. The consumer's work appears as an unrelated trace.
diagram:
traceparent: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-01
  ↓ HTTP header ✓ usually automatic
  ↓ message header ✗ usually forgotten

Broken propagation = orphaned traces

means: Alert on what users experience, not on internal causes. Cause-based alerts fire constantly and miss the failures you didn't predict.
example: 'CPU > 80%' pages during a harmless batch job. 'Checkout success rate < 99%' pages only when users are actually hurting.
diagram:
Cause-based:   CPU high, pod restarted, disk 70%
  → noisy, misses novel failures

Symptom-based: error rate, latency SLI,
  checkout success → always matters ✓

means: For every resource, track Utilisation, Saturation and Errors. The counterpart to RED for CPU, memory, disk and pools.
example: CPU utilisation at 60% looks fine until you check saturation — the run queue is 12 deep, so processes are waiting despite 'spare' CPU.
diagram:
U  Utilisation  % busy
S  Saturation   queued work waiting ← the useful one
E  Errors       failed operations

Applies to: CPU, memory, disk, network, conn pools
